lead: A display instrument turns an electrical quantity into a number or a trace. Numbers suit slow, accurate measurements; traces suit waveforms and one-time events. Every display trades accuracy, bandwidth and capture ability. This chapter covers the DVM, CRO, DSO and spectrum analyser, and the numbers that describe them.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.9 for the amplifiers and filters ahead of a display, and Unit 1 for accuracy and resolution.

blocks.text: A digital voltmeter (DVM) converts an input voltage into a display number. The display has N counts, which fixes resolution: it splits the full-scale range into N steps.

blocks.where: range is the full-scale voltage of the selected range, in V; counts is the number of steps the display can show; resolution is the smallest voltage change the display can show, in V.

blocks.text: A 3½ digit display has three full digits and one half digit that is only 0 or 1. Largest reading 1999, so 2000 counts. A 4½ digit meter has 20 000 counts. The sign is separate.

Accuracy is quoted against reading, not range. The counts term is fixed last-digit uncertainty; the percentage term is gain error that grows with reading. Near full scale the percentage term dominates; near zero the counts term dominates. Use the lowest range that does not overload.

items: Ramp DVM: a ramp starts and a counter runs; the input stops the counter. Voltage becomes time, counted.
Integrating DVM: integrates input over a whole number of mains cycles (100 ms at 50 Hz). Mains hum integrates to zero.
Autozero: meter measures its own offset with input shorted and subtracts it.

blocks.text: A multimeter adds current, resistance and continuity. On voltage ranges the input looks like about 10 MΩ, so a high-resistance source reads low. On current ranges a shunt inserts burden voltage, lost from the circuit.

sections.h3: CRO: CRT deflection and block diagram

blocks.text: The cathode ray tube (CRT) is a vacuum glass envelope. An electron gun fires a thin beam at a phosphor screen; the phosphor glows where the beam lands. Two plate pairs deflect it: vertical plates stacked one above the other push up/down; horizontal plates side by side push left/right. This is electrostatic deflection.

blocks.where: D is spot deflection on the screen, in m; L is distance from plate centre to screen; l is plate length; d is plate separation; Vd is voltage between the plates; Va is accelerating voltage; S is deflection sensitivity, in m/V. S falls as Va rises, so a brighter, faster beam needs more amplifier gain.

blocks.text: The panel quotes volts per division. The vertical channel is an attenuator (V/div switch) then a vertical amplifier driving vertical plates. The horizontal channel is a time base generating a linear ramp, then a horizontal amplifier driving horizontal plates. The ramp sweeps the spot once per ramp, so time becomes horizontal distance.

A trigger starts the ramp only when the input crosses a chosen level in a chosen direction. A repeating waveform then stands still. A ×10 probe divides the input by ten before the attenuator, so multiply the panel reading by ten to get actual input.

blocks.where: T is one sweep time in s; time/div is the panel setting in s/div; divisions is the number of horizontal divisions the sweep covers (usually 10); f is the frequency of the displayed waveform in Hz.

blocks.text: A digital storage oscilloscope (DSO) replaces phosphor with an ADC, memory and screen. The input passes the same attenuator and amplifier, is sampled at sampling rate fs, stored in N samples, and drawn from memory.
record time = (time/div) × divisions,   N = fs × record time,   fmax = fs / 2
blocks.where: record time is the captured time in s; fs is sampling rate in samples per second; N is record length, the number of stored samples; fmax is the highest frequency the record can show without aliasing, in Hz.

blocks.text: Sampling below 2f, where f is signal frequency, folds the signal to a false low frequency: aliasing. The trace looks stable and is wrong. Raise fs above 2f (Nyquist limit) or use the bandwidth limit filter.
Pre-trigger stores samples from before the trigger, so you see what caused an event. With single-shot capture, a DSO catches a one-time glitch a CRT would miss.

The spectrum analyser displays amplitude against frequency. A swept superheterodyne type mixes input with a swept local oscillator, passes the difference through a band-pass filter of width RBW (resolution bandwidth), detects and plots it. Span is the frequency range shown. Narrow RBW separates close tones and lowers noise floor, but the sweep must be slower. An FFT analyser digitises a block and computes a fast Fourier transform, giving the whole spectrum at once.

figure.caption: Signal path through an oscilloscope: the attenuator and vertical amplifier set volts per division, the triggered time base sets seconds per division, and the two plate pairs deflect the beam on the phosphor screen.

spec.title: CRO block diagram
spec.aria: A CRO block diagram: the input goes through attenuator and vertical amplifier to the vertical plates, the triggered time base drives the horizontal amplifier and horizontal plates, and both plate pairs act on the CRT screen.

examples.question: A 3½ digit DVM on the 2 V range has 2000 counts and accuracy ±(0.5% of reading + 2 counts). It reads 1.000 V. Find resolution and error. A DSO is set to 1 µs/div over 10 divisions and samples at 100 MS/s; find record time and record length.
steps: Resolution = range / counts = 2 V / 2000 = 0.001 V = 1 mV. One count is 1 mV.
Percentage term = 0.5% of 1.000 V = 0.005 × 1.000 V = 5 mV.
Total error = 5 mV + 2 mV = 7 mV, so true value lies in 1.000 V ± 7 mV.
Record time = (time/div) × divisions = 1 µs/div × 10 div = 10 µs.
Record length N = fs × record time = 100 × 10⁶ samples/s × 10 × 10⁻⁶ s = 1000 samples.
Highest frequency shown without aliasing = fs/2 = 50 MHz.
examples.answer: Resolution 1 mV; error ±7 mV on a 1.000 V reading; DSO record time 10 µs holding a record length of 1000 samples.
examples.check:
counts = 2000
rng = 2.0
res = rng / counts
reading = 1.000
err = 0.005 * reading + 2 * res
fs = 100e6
t_div = 1e-6
divs = 10
record = t_div * divs
N = fs * record
print(res * 1e3)
print(err * 1e3)
print(record * 1e6)
print(N)

traps: A 3½ digit display has 2000 counts (largest reading 1999), not 3000. On the 2 V range one count is 1 mV.
The counts term is counts of the least significant digit on the range in use, so its value changes with range.
If a DSO samples below twice the signal frequency, the trace folds to a false low frequency; it looks stable and is wrong. Check fs against 2f.
The V/div setting ignores the probe. With a ×10 probe, 3.2 div peak-to-peak at 2 V/div is 3.2 × 2 × 10 = 64 V, not 6.4 V.
On a swept spectrum analyser a wide RBW hides two close tones as one peak, and noise floor depends on RBW, so compare spectra at the same RBW.

quiz.q: What is a 3½ digit DVM display, and how many counts does it have?
quiz.a: Three full digits 0-9 and one half digit only 0 or 1. Largest reading 1999, so 2000 counts.

quiz.q: Why does an integrating DVM reject 50 Hz mains hum?
quiz.a: It integrates over a fixed window equal to a whole number of mains cycles (100 ms at 50 Hz), so hum halves cancel.

quiz.q: A 4½ digit DVM has 20 000 counts, 20 V range, accuracy ±(0.1% of reading + 3 counts). It reads 5.000 V. Find resolution and error.
quiz.a: Resolution = 20/20 000 = 1 mV; 3 counts = 3 mV; percentage term = 0.001 × 5.000 = 5 mV; error = 5 + 3 = 8 mV, so 5.000 V ± 8 mV.

quiz.q: A CRO set to 2 V/div shows a 3.2 division peak-to-peak trace with a ×10 probe connected. What is the input peak-to-peak voltage?
quiz.a: 3.2 div × 2 V/div = 6.4 V on screen; the probe divides by 10, so input is 6.4 × 10 = 64 V peak-to-peak.

quiz.q: A DSO samples at 200 MS/s with 5 µs/div over 10 divisions. Find record time, record length and highest unaliased frequency, and say what a 150 MHz sine will look like.
quiz.a: Record time = 5 µs/div × 10 = 50 µs; N = 200 × 10⁶ × 50 × 10⁻⁶ = 10 000 samples; fmax = 100 MHz. The 150 MHz sine aliases to |200 − 150| = 50 MHz and appears as a stable but false 50 MHz trace.

quiz.q: What is the use of pre-trigger in a DSO?
quiz.a: It keeps samples from before the trigger point, so the cause of a glitch is captured along with the event.

quiz.q: A swept spectrum analyser shows two tones 5 kHz apart. What happens as RBW is changed from 30 kHz to 1 kHz, and what is the cost?
quiz.a: At 30 kHz RBW the two tones merge into one peak, since RBW exceeds their spacing. At 1 kHz RBW they resolve as two peaks and the noise floor drops, but the sweep must be slower to cover the same span.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern bench instruments are mostly digitising: fast ADC plus memory replaces CRT and swept filter, and FFT does spectrum in software. The chain is attenuator, amplifier, ADC, DSP, display. Old figures of merit become sampling rate, memory depth and effective number of bits. Mixed-signal scopes add logic channels; USB and PXI modules put the display on a laptop. Search for effective number of bits, digital phosphor display, real-time spectrum analyser and resolution bandwidth.
